# Dynamic Scene and Temporal Modeling

Also called: Dynamic NeRF, 4D NeRF, Temporal NeRF

## Overview
Dynamic Scene and Temporal Modeling extends static Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) to handle non-rigid motion and time-varying scenes, solving the problem of rendering novel views of environments that change over time [S1]. Unlike static methods, these approaches introduce temporal dimensions to the radiance field representation, either by warping coordinates to a canonical space, directly conditioning on time, or using explicit deformation fields [S1]. This family is distinguished from static NeRF variants by its ability to model temporal dynamics, setting it apart from siblings like [Model Architecture Modifications](11313-model-architecture-modifications.md) which focus on spatial representation improvements without inherent temporal handling.

## Shared principles
All methods in this family share the goal of reconstructing a 4D radiance field $R(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}, t)$ that maps 3D spatial coordinates $\mathbf{x}$, viewing direction $\mathbf{d}$, and time $t$ to volume density $\sigma$ and color $\mathbf{c}$. The core challenge is resolving the ambiguity between camera motion and object motion. Most methods achieve this by establishing a **canonical space** (a static reference frame) and learning a **deformation field** or **warping function** that maps dynamic coordinates $\mathbf{x}$ at time $t$ to their canonical counterparts $\mathbf{x}'$. The radiance field is then queried in this canonical space, which is static, allowing standard NeRF rendering techniques to be applied. Alternatively, some methods bypass warping by directly conditioning the MLP on the time coordinate $t$. The rendering equation remains the standard volume rendering integral, but density and color are now functions of time:
$$ C(\mathbf{r}, t) = \int_{s_n}^{s_f} T(s, t) \sigma(\mathbf{r}(s), t) c(\mathbf{r}(s), \mathbf{d}, t) ds $$
where $T(s, t) = \exp \left( -\int_{s_n}^{s} \sigma(\mathbf{r}(s'), t) ds' \right)$ [S1].

## Subtopics

### [Gear-NeRF](13848-gear-nerf.md)
Gear-NeRF stratifies the scene into motion-based 'gears' using semantic information, allowing region-specific spatio-temporal sampling resolution. It solves the inefficiency of uniform high-resolution sampling in dynamic scenes by assigning higher-resolution gears to regions with larger motion scales. Unlike unified 4D volumes, it uses parallel 4D feature volumes per gear level, determined by a learned semantic embedding.

### [NeRF with Time Parameter](14705-nerf-with-time-parameter.md)
This method adapts static NeRF by augmenting the input domain with a temporal coordinate $t$. It serves as a baseline for temporal modeling by treating time as a direct input feature, avoiding complex deformation fields. It is distinguished by its simplicity but suffers from blurriness and ghosting artifacts compared to warping-based methods.

### [Forward Warping for Novel View Synthesis](15541-forward-warping-for-novel-view-synthesis.md)
This method models a static scene at a canonical time step and forward warps the entire radiance field to other time steps using average splatting and an inpaint network. It addresses many-to-one mapping difficulties inherent in dynamic reconstruction, achieving superior performance for canonical frames compared to backward flow methods.

### [Dynamic Appearance Particle Neural Radiance Field](15550-dynamic-appearance-particle-neural-radiance-field.md)
This method superimposes a static grid-based radiance field with a particle-based dynamic field, applying particles only to dynamic elements. It solves non-rigid motion capture without prior geometric knowledge, distinguishing itself from ParticleNeRF by using linear interpolation on a grid for efficient querying.

### [KFD-NeRF](15551-kfd-nerf.md)
KFD-NeRF models the 4D radiance field as a dynamic system estimated using a Kalman filter, separating motion estimation into an observer branch (direct observation) and a predictor branch (history-based prediction). It differs from Gear-NeRF and NeRF with Time Parameter by using smoother deformation fields and a tri-plane spatial representation for faster convergence.

### [SLS4D](16576-sls4d.md)
SLS4D represents dynamic scenes using a sparse, compact latent feature space, replacing dense voxel grids to reduce parameters while maintaining quality. It distinguishes itself by abandoning direct coordinate-based feature determination in favor of relative relationships in a learned latent space, utilizing an attention mechanism.

#### ER-NeRF
- **Definition:** A Conditional NeRF framework for effective, high-accuracy dynamic portrait creation, producing dynamic portrait videos synchronized with audio [S1].
- **Steps:** Utilizes spatial regions’ distinct contributions to steer dynamic head modeling; develops a concise and articulate Tri-Plane Hash Representation; introduces rapid and straightforward Adaptive Pose Encoding to enhance the separation of the head and torso [S1].
- **Pitfalls:** Additional fine-tuning might be necessary to sustain superior rendering outcomes for poses that exceed the scope of the training dataset [S1].
- **Numbers:** Attains instantaneous rendering and rapid convergence using a compact model size [S1].

#### NeRF-MS
- **Definition:** A method that diminishes vagueness in visual alterations by implementing a ternary loss to standardize the spread of visual codes across each image [S1].
- **Steps:** Suggests a temporary decomposition unit to more effectively distinguish still scenes from dynamic objects [S1].
- **Pitfalls:** Might encounter difficulties in managing significant sequence discrepancies, like severe alterations in the visual aspect of scenes caused by the activation of lights [S1].
- **Numbers:** Trials using both real-life outdoor and artificial datasets reveal that NeRF-MS attains cutting-edge results in multi-sequence scenarios, markedly enhancing rendering efficiency through the reconstruction of 3D-consistent visuals and minimizing ghost effects [S1].

## Background
The concept of dynamic scene modeling in NeRF originated with D-NeRF, which introduced deformation fields to warp dynamic points to a canonical space [S1]. Subsequent works like HyperNeRF and others expanded on this by introducing hierarchical representations, forward warping techniques, and particle-based systems to handle complex non-rigid motions [S1]. The field has evolved to include semantic-aware stratification (Gear-NeRF), Kalman filtering for temporal consistency (KFD-NeRF), and sparse latent representations (SLS4D) to improve efficiency and quality [S1]. These methods are primarily used in 3D reconstruction, novel view synthesis, and dynamic portrait generation [S1].
